About this project

# Lineup intelligence as transparent decision support

 This app is built for people who care about
 **how five players function as a unit**—not only
 who tops a sortable table, but which combinations actually earn minutes, which efficient groups stay
 under-used, and how a single substitution might shift the statistical profile of a lineup.

## 1. The basketball problem

 NBA lineup data is **noisy, context-dependent, and hard
 to operationalize** for rotation decisions. A five-man net rating tells you how that group performed in
 the minutes they shared—but not _why_, not against whom, and not whether the sample is stable enough to
 trust.

- **Raw net rating is insufficient alone.** It
 compresses offense and defense, hides minute totals, and rewards small samples that can swing with a few hot
 shooting nights.

- **Sample size is relentless.** Rare lineups can
 look elite or awful by variance. The product uses minute floors and explicit scoring rules so users choose
 how much noise they tolerate.

- **Rotations are tradeoffs.** Staggering stars,
 preserving spacing, hiding a weak defender, or closing with a defensive shell—all of that is a sequence of
 lineup choices, not one “best five.”

- **Role overlap and substitution shape identity.**
 Replacing one connector with another changes ball pressure, rim protection, and shot profile even when
 “talent” looks similar on paper.

## 2. Why lineup analysis matters

 Playoffs shorten rotations; matchups invite different frontiers; spacing and defensive versatility decide whether
 an offense can breathe; stagger patterns determine whether a star carries a weak bench or plays next to another
 creator. Lineup-level analysis is where
 **offensive identity meets defensive coverage tradeoffs
 **—where coaching staff actually live during games.

 Public tools often stop at player cards. This product keeps the
 **five-man unit** as the primary object so
 conversations about “this group” stay grounded in observed combinations and minutes, not hypothetical mixes.

## 3. What the app attempts to solve

 The goal is **not** to perfectly predict future lineup performance. It is to offer a
 **transparent framework** for comparing lineup
 efficiency, usage patterns, and substitution dynamics—so analysts can triage questions, communicate tradeoffs,
 and stress-test intuition with interpretable numbers.

In practice, the app supports workflows like:

- Ranking and filtering units by net, offensive or defensive rating, minutes, or the composite Underrated Lineup Score you will see soon.

- Contrasting “best on paper” efficiency with “most used” groups—the rotation story versus the efficiency story.

- Running a directional substitution heuristic from an observed lineup baseline.

### What coaches and ops might care about

 The UI invites **operational language**: not “this
 model says win,” but “this unit sacrifices rim protection for spacing,” “this group posts strong efficiency but
 rarely plays together,” “this swap steepens the playmaking gradient while thinning perimeter pressure.” Those
 interpretations remain _human-led_; the app supplies structured signals so the story stays anchored in
 data you can inspect.

## 4. Methodological philosophy

- **Transparency over black boxes.** Weights and
 simulator coefficients are stated here and in code configuration.

- **Interpretability over overfitting.** Simple
 transforms (min–max, explicit deltas) beat opaque scores that cannot be defended in a staff meeting.

- **Directional signals.** Outputs are heuristics and
 comparisons—not calibrated win forecasts.

- **Operational usability.** Filters, exports, and
 team views prioritize prep questions: who plays, who’s efficient, who’s under-used, what-if this swap.

How that becomes numbers

 The sections below are the **technical specification**

 League numbers vs app-only calculations

- **Tables & leaderboards (Net, ORtg, DRtg, Pace):**
 For live NBA ingest, these are **read from NBA.com**
 (`OFF_RATING`, `DEF_RATING`,
 `NET_RATING`, `PACE`, etc.) and
 stored as-is. This product **does not replace** the league’s lineup **NET_RATING** with
 its own alternate “true net” for those views.

- **ULS:** A **separate composite score**
 built from normalized inputs (including the ingested `net_rating` column).
 It is not an NBA-published statistic.

- **Substitution simulator:** The
 `ProjOff`, `ProjDef`, and
 `ProjNet` formulas below are **this app’s heuristic only**,
 run when you simulate a swap. **ProjNet is not the same
 field** as the **Net** column in lineup tables—it is “projected net after the stated
 player deltas,” not the league’s historical `NET_RATING` for the
 original five.

## Data and season scope

- **Season:** `2025-26`,
 **NBA regular season only** (no playoffs, play-in,
 preseason, or All-Star) in all `nba_api` pulls.

- **Primary path:** live ingestion from NBA Stats
 into SQLite when you run `python -m data_pipeline.ingest_all`. The UI
 exposes `GET /api/scope` so you can confirm the stored source (e.g.
 `nba_stats_api`).

- **Optional demo:**
 `python -m data_pipeline.ingest_all --seed` loads synthetic lineups
 for offline UI work only—not real minutes or real five-man combinations.

- **Storage:** SQLite today; schema is written to
 be portable toward PostgreSQL if you outgrow a single file.

## Pace, possessions, and efficiency columns

 The app ingests NBA.com advanced summaries. In the tables you will see **efficiency**, **volume**, and
 **tempo** on different scales—mixing them up is a
 common source of confusion.

- **Offensive rating (ORtg) & defensive rating (DRtg):**
 For teams and five-man lineups in this build, these come from the league feed configured for
 **per-100-possession** reporting—i.e. expected
 points scored (ORtg) or allowed (DRtg) _per 100 possessions_ for that row. They answer “how efficient
 per possession,” not “how many points per game.”

- **Net rating (tables):** The
 **NET_RATING** value from the same NBA.com lineup
 (or team) row—**ingested directly**, not recomputed
 by this app for live data. It is on the same per-100 scale as ORtg/DRtg and is conceptually “offensive minus
 defensive efficiency” for that unit; the UI shows the league’s number, not a custom replacement.

- **Pace:** The **Pace** field on a **team** or **lineup** row is the league’s **tempo** statistic for that entity: in standard NBA.com presentation it reads as an estimate of
 **possessions per 48 minutes** (full regulation
 length). **Higher pace ⇒ more possessions per 48** for that unit’s time on the floor. It does
 _not_ measure shot-making quality by itself—pair pace with ORtg/DRtg/Net and with minutes to interpret
 small samples.

- **Possessions column (lineups):** When the API
 provides lineup possessions we store them; otherwise the pipeline may approximate from minutes and pace-style
 signals for downstream use (e.g. ULS). Check raw minutes alongside any derived possession estimate.

## Minute floors (what each screen asks for)

 There is **no single global cutoff**. Each view
 requests lineups with at least **X** minutes played _together_; **X** differs by
 page and URL parameters.

- **Leaderboard** defaults to
 **50** minutes (slider can change it), aligned with ULS eligibility so the table usually shows
 scores instead of blanks. The API default for generic lineup lists matches that product choice when
 `min_minutes` is omitted.

- **Home** uses high floors (often 80–100) for
 featured samples so cards are not dominated by tiny-sample noise.

- **Team explorer** uses different floors per
 column: e.g. **50** for “best net,” **40** for the ORtg–DRtg scatter sample,
 **0** for “most minutes,” and **50** for “most underrated (ULS)” so every row in
 that slice has a computed ULS (same threshold as the score itself).

- **Substitution simulator** uses
 **30** minutes minimum for lineup choices (so the dropdown still has options without ultra-rare
 groups), and loads up to **100** of that team’s heaviest-minute lineups for the menu.

- **Underrated (ULS) page** defaults to
 **50** minutes for the list; the slider cannot go below 50 because
 **ULS is undefined below that floor** (see ULS section).

## Lineup fit traits (spacing, playmaking, defense, rebounding)

 These are **descriptive** scores built from the five
 roster players attached to a lineup row: shooting mix, assist and turnover signals, steal/block activity and
 DBPM (Defensive Box Plus/Minus) proxies, and rebound volume. Each raw trait column is computed for every lineup, then
 **winsorized at the 2nd and 98th percentiles** and
 scaled to **0–100 with min–max** across the league lineup population in the database at enrichment
 time.

 Traits **do not drive ULS** and are not winsorized
 inside the ULS formula—they help you _describe_ a unit next to efficiency numbers, not replace them.

## Underrated Lineup Score (ULS)—explicit definition

 **Eligibility.** Only lineups with
 **minutes ≥ 50** enter the ULS calculation. Everyone else gets a missing ULS (shown as “—” in the
 UI).

 **Normalization `norm(x)`.**
 For each ingredient below, take all _eligible_ lineups (minutes ≥ 50), collect that ingredient’s values,
 and apply **pure min–max to 0–100** on that set:
 `100 × (x − min) / (max − min)`. There is
 **no winsorization inside ULS**. If `max == min` for an
 ingredient, every lineup receives **50** for that ingredient (avoids divide-by-zero).

 **Defensive rating (lower is better).** Before
 normalizing, defensive rating is **negated** so that better defense (lower DRtg) maps to a higher
 value after scaling: use `−defensive_rating` inside
 `norm`.

 **Limited Usage Bonus (LUB)—two steps.** Among
 eligible minutes (≥ 50) only:

- Raw bonus:
 `
 LUB_raw = 1 − (minutes − min(minutes)) / (max(minutes) − min(minutes))
 `
 . Fewer minutes together ⇒ higher `LUB_raw`. If all eligible
 lineups share the same minute total, `LUB_raw = 1` for all.

- Then **normalize again**: `norm(LUB_raw)` to 0–100
 across the same eligible set—so the “usage” axis is comparable to the other ingredients.

 **Possessions.** If a lineup row lacks
 possessions, the pipeline uses `minutes × 2` as a fallback before
 `norm`.

 **Final ULS** is the weighted sum of the five normalized
 ingredients (weights sum to 1):

```
ULS =
 0.35 × norm(net_rating)
 + 0.20 × norm(offensive_rating)
 + 0.20 × norm(−defensive_rating)
 + 0.15 × norm(LUB_raw) ← LUB_raw from the two-step LUB above; this is the second min–max
 + 0.10 × norm(possessions)
```

What each weight is doing

 Weights are a **fixed product spec** (they sum to
 **1.0**) applied _after_ each ingredient is
 scaled to 0–100 on the eligible lineup set. They are not re-fit from data inside the app.

- **0.35 on net rating** — largest slice: overall
 per-possession margin (ORtg − DRtg on the row) is the single best summary of how good the unit was, so it
 anchors the score.

- **0.20 on offensive rating** — keeps
 _offensive efficiency_ visible on its own, not only through net (e.g. elite offense dragged by defense
 in a small sample still registers).

- **0.20 on inverted defensive rating** — same-sized
 slice for _defensive efficiency_, after negating DRtg so lower allowed (better defense) scores higher
 once normalized.

- **0.15 on LUB** — the “underrated” axis among
 lineups that already cleared the minutes gate: fewer shared minutes within the qualified pool nudges the
 composite up versus peers with similar efficiency on heavier run.

- **0.10 on possessions** — a modest volume
 tiebreaker so all else equal, lineups with more documented opportunity can separate from extreme low-minute
 outliers; small enough that the score does not become “who plays the most.”

## Substitution simulator—explicit definition

 **Important:** Everything in this section is
 **only** for the simulator output. The **Net** (and ORtg/DRtg) you see in lineup
 tables elsewhere still come from **NBA Stats ingestion** until you run a simulation—then the API
 returns _additional_ projected fields alongside those baselines. See also
 [League numbers vs app-only calculations](#league-vs-app-metrics)
 .

 Start from the **observed lineup** offensive and
 defensive ratings (`CurrentOff`, `CurrentDef`
 )—those baselines are the **same NBA-sourced ORtg/DRtg**
 already stored for that lineup. Then apply **this app’s**
 player-in vs player-out deltas on OBPM (Offensive Box Plus/Minus), TS% (True Shooting Percentage), AST%
 (Assist Percentage), TOV% (Turnover Percentage), DBPM (Defensive Box Plus/Minus), STL% (Steal Percentage), and
 BLK% (Block Percentage). Percent stats must be
 **decimals** (e.g. true shooting
 `0.58`, not `58`).

 **Projected offensive rating**

```
ProjOff = CurrentOff
 + 1.8 × (OBPM_in − OBPM_out)
 + 8.0 × (TS_in − TS_out)
 + 0.12 × (ASTpct_in − ASTpct_out)
 − 0.08 × (TOVpct_in − TOVpct_out)
```

Coefficients on projected offense

 These are **linear sensitivities** in
 **points per 100 possessions** on the lineup’s
 projected ORtg for each one-unit change in the player swap (they do _not_ sum to 1 like ULS weights).
 Percent stats are **decimals** (e.g. 0.58 TS%).

- **+1.8 × ΔOBPM** — OBPM is on a BPM-style
 scale; each full point of OBPM edge for the incoming player lifts projected ORtg by about 1.8 per 100 at the
 margin.

- **+8.0 × ΔTS** — true shooting moves in tiny
 decimals, so the coefficient is large: a +0.01 TS edge (one percentage point expressed as 0.01) shifts
 projected ORtg by about **+0.08** per 100 through
 this term alone.

- **+0.12 × ΔAST%** — assist percentage as a
 decimal; a +0.05 gap (five percentage points as 0.05) adds about
 **+0.006** ORtg per 100 through this channel.

- **−0.08 × ΔTOV%** — turnover percentage as a
 decimal; the leading minus means a higher incoming TOV% _hurts_ projected offense (more dead
 possessions).

 **Projected defensive rating** (lower allowed is better)

```
ProjDef = CurrentDef
 − 1.5 × (DBPM_in − DBPM_out)
 − 0.10 × (STLpct_in − STLpct_out)
 − 0.10 × (BLKpct_in − BLKpct_out)
```

Coefficients on projected defense

 `CurrentDef` is points allowed per 100 (lower is better). Each term
 below **subtracts** from
 `CurrentDef`, so a positive swap delta in a “good” defensive signal
 lowers projected points allowed.

- **−1.5 × ΔDBPM** — DBPM on a BPM-style scale;
 about 1.5 points per 100 allowed shaved off for each full point of DBPM improvement in the swap.

- **−0.10 × ΔSTL%** — steal rate as a decimal
 (e.g. 0.02); a +0.01 gap moves this layer by 0.10 × 0.01 =
 **0.001** on the projected allowed scale (small
 next to DBPM, but directionally rewards higher steal activity).

- **−0.10 × ΔBLK%** — block rate as a decimal,
 same multiplier as steals: a +0.01 gap contributes 0.001 through this term alone; DBPM still carries most
 of the defensive shift in typical swaps.

 **Projected net rating**

```
ProjNet = ProjOff − ProjDef
```

 **No extra weights here:**
 `ProjNet` is simply the spread between the two projected per-100 ratings
 above—the same ORtg − DRtg idea applied to _projected_ offense and defense, not another weighted blend.

 `ProjNet` is **not** a
 relabeled copy of the league’s lineup `NET_RATING`. It is the difference
 between two _projected_ per-100-style ratings produced only by the formulas above. The historical
 **Net** column in the rest of the app is unchanged by this calculation.

 There is **no shrink toward team ratings** in this
 build—the projection is entirely the lineup baseline plus the stated deltas.

## What’s in the product (routes)

- **Leaderboard** — League-wide lineup table: sort, search, minute floors, CSV export.

- **Team explorer** — Within-team contrasts: high net vs heavy minutes vs ULS-ranked samples.

- **Underrated** — Sortable ULS view: minutes floor is ≥ 50 (same as ULS computation—scores are blank below that).

- **Substitution simulator** — Swap one roster player into a selected observed lineup; see projected ORtg/DRtg/net and narrative summary.

## Limitations (read this)

 Building trust means stating what the app **does not** know. Treat every insight as conditional on
 these constraints:

- **Context dependence:** opponent strength, home/road, garbage time, and
 game script are not layered into the public lineup tables this build consumes.

- **No player tracking:** no second-spectrum spacing pressure, close-out
 speed, or pick-and-roll coverage tags—only what box-style and advanced summaries approximate.

- **No scheme labels:** the app does not classify “switch everything” vs
 “drop” vs “ice”; defensive rating is an outcome, not a playbook.

- **No injury or availability modeling:** substitutions are statistical
 thought experiments, not workload or medical recommendations.

- **Survivorship and selection:** coaches pick who plays together;
 observed lineups reflect those choices, not random assignment.

- **Public data caps:** ingestion may not return every theoretical five-man
 combination league-wide—only what the upstream feed exposes for the configured season and season type.

- **Player proxies:** when true BPM is unavailable from the feed, OBPM
 (Offensive Box Plus/Minus) and DBPM (Defensive Box Plus/Minus) may be proxied from offensive/defensive rating
 vs league quantiles during ingestion—noisy, but documented as a transparency tradeoff.

## Future directions

 A natural roadmap—especially with richer data—includes matchup-aware projections, possession-level weighting
 (clutch vs garbage), defensive coverage or ball-screen taxonomy, transition frequency modeling,
 opponent-specific lineup recommendations, and eventually player-tracking integration. A dedicated case-study
 write-up (one team’s rotation efficiency vs usage, tied to film) would further bridge engineering and
 storytelling.
